prompt: Anh, Ben and Chen have 30 balls altogether. If Ben gives 5 balls to Chen, Chen gives 4 balls to Anh and Anh gives 2 balls to Ben, then the three boys will have an equal number of balls. How many balls did Anh have at first?

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
At the end each boy has $30 \div 3 = 10$ balls. Anh received 4 and gave away 2, a net gain of 2, so he started with $10 - 2 = 8$.

**Answer: (A) 8**

prompt: A regular die has a total of 7 points on any two of its opposite faces. In the figure, two regular dice are placed as shown. What is the sum of the points on all invisible faces of the dice?

When announcing the results of a raffle, the moderator said: “The winning tickets are those which contain a number with at least 5 digits such that at most three of its digits are greater than 2.” Subsequently, the speaker drew tickets with the numbers 1022, 22222, 102334, 213343, 3042531. How many of them were winning ones?

solutions.title: Check each ticket
solutions.body:
- 1022: only 4 digits ✗
- 22222: no digit above 2 ✓
- 102334: digits above 2 are 3, 3, 4 — three ✓
- 213343: 3, 3, 4, 3 — four ✗
- 3042531: 3, 4, 5, 3 — four ✗

Two winning tickets.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: In the triangle $ABC$, $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $E$ is the midpoint of $DB$ and $F$ is the midpoint of $BC$. If the area of triangle $ABC$ is 96, what is the area of triangle $AEF$?

solutions.title: Two halvings
solutions.body:
$F$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $[ABF] = \frac12[ABC] = 48$. Triangles $AEF$ and $ABF$ have the same height from $F$, and $AE = \frac34 AB$ (since $AD = \frac12 AB$ and $DE = \frac14 AB$). So $[AEF] = \frac34\cdot 48 = 36$.

**Answer: (D) 36**

solutions.title: Subtract
solutions.body:
$[EBF] = \frac14[ABF] = 12$ because $EB = \frac14 AB$. Then $[AEF] = [ABF] - [EBF] = 48 - 12 = 36$.

**Answer: (D) 36**

prompt: Frida has 2007 marbles kept in three bags, A, B and C. Each bag contains the same number of marbles. If Frida moves $\frac23$ of the marbles in bag A to bag C, what will be the ratio between the number of marbles in bag A and bag C?

solutions.title: Use thirds of a bag
solutions.body:
Each bag has 669 marbles; call one third of a bag a "part" (223 marbles). Bag A keeps 1 part; bag C has 3 parts plus 2 more parts = 5 parts. Ratio $1 : 5$.

**Answer: (D) 1:5**

prompt: An international organisation has 32 members. It is predicted that the organisation will increase the number of its members by 50% each year. How many members will the organisation have in three years?

solutions.title: Year by year
solutions.body:
$32 \to 48 \to 72 \to 108$ (each year multiply by $1.5$).

**Answer: (C) 108**

solutions.title: One multiplication
solutions.body:
$32\cdot\left(\frac32\right)^3 = 32\cdot\frac{27}{8} = 108$.

**Answer: (C) 108**

prompt: In one move, the King can go to any adjacent square, along a row, column, or diagonal. How many routes with the minimum number of moves are there for the king to travel from the top left square to the bottom right square on the grid?

solutions.title: Where to put the straight move
solutions.body:
The grid has 4 columns and 5 rows, so the king must go 3 squares right and 4 squares down. Every move goes at most one row down, so at least 4 moves are needed, and 4 moves suffice: each move goes down one row, and exactly 3 of them also go one column right (diagonal moves) while one goes straight down.

A shortest route is determined by which of the 4 moves is the straight one: 4 routes.

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: What is the least possible value of the expression $2007 - KAN - GA - ROO$, if it is given that each letter represents a digit (different letters represent different digits and the same letters equal digits)?

solutions.title: Maximise the sum
solutions.body:
We want $KAN + GA + ROO$ as large as possible:
$$KAN + GA + ROO = 100(K + R) + 11A + 11O + 10G + N.$$
Give the largest digits to the largest coefficients: $K, R = 9, 8$ (200-coefficient total), then $A, O = 7, 6$, then $G = 5$, then $N = 4$:
$$1700 + 11\cdot 13 + 50 + 4 = 1897.$$
E.g. $974 + 57 + 866 = 1897$. The least value is $2007 - 1897 = 110$.

**Answer: (B) 110**

prompt: In the diagram, the triangle $ABC$ is divided into nine non-overlapping sections by drawing two lines from each of the vertices $A$ and $B$. How many non-overlapping sections will there be if four lines are drawn from each of these vertices?

solutions.title: Strips cut by strips
solutions.body:
The four lines from $A$ divide the triangle into 5 "fans" from $A$. Each line from $B$ crosses every fan, cutting it into one more piece: the 4 lines from $B$ cut each fan into 5 pieces. Total $5\cdot 5 = 25$ (with 2 lines each: $3\cdot 3 = 9$ ✓).

**Answer: (B) 25**

solutions.title: Count by adding lines
solutions.body:
Start with the 5 pieces from $A$'s lines. Each line from $B$ crosses the 4 lines from $A$, so it is cut into 5 segments, each splitting a region in two: $+5$ regions per line. $5 + 4\cdot 5 = 25$.

**Answer: (B) 25**

prompt: An island is inhabited by liars and nobles (the liars always tell lies and the nobles always tell the truth). One day, 12 islanders, among them both liars and nobles, gathered together and made a few statements. Two people said: “Exactly two people among us twelve are liars”. Another four people said: “Exactly four people among us twelve are liars”. The remaining six people said: “Exactly six people among us twelve are liars”. How many liars were there?

solutions.title: Only one group can be right
solutions.body:
The three statements contradict each other, so at most one group tells the truth, and since there are nobles, exactly one group does — all others are liars.
- If the 2 people were right, there would be 10 liars, not 2. ✗
- If the 4 people were right, there would be 8 liars, not 4. ✗
- If the 6 people were right, there are 6 liars ✓.

So there are 6 liars.

**Answer: (C) 6**

prompt: A hallway is sagged on the right side. As a consequence, the profile is no longer a rectangle but a parallelogram. There is a door halfway through the hallway. The door has two sections, which can be opened separately. Where should they put the hinges?

choices.text: The door can never open properly

solutions.title: Watch the floor and the ceiling
solutions.body:
The floor and the ceiling slope down towards the right; the door sections have vertical sides and sloping top and bottom edges. A section turns about a vertical hinge, so every point of it keeps its height while it moves closer to the hinge side (seen across the hallway).

- **Lower section:** its bottom edge lies on the floor. If the hinge is on the left, the points of the bottom edge move to the left, where the floor is higher — the door scrapes the floor. With the hinge on the right they move right, where the floor is lower: it opens freely.
- **Upper section:** its top edge is at the ceiling. With the hinge on the right its points move right, where the ceiling is lower — it jams. With the hinge on the left they move to where the ceiling is higher: fine.

So: hinges above on the left, below on the right.

**Answer: (C) above left, below right**

prompt: A 10 m rope is fastened to one of the corners of a house, which has the form of a rectangle 6 m long and 4 m wide. A dog is fastened to the rope. What is the perimeter of the region that the dog can access?

solutions.title: Three arcs
solutions.body:
Outside the house the dog can sweep $\frac34$ of a circle of radius 10 around the corner: length $\frac34\cdot 2\pi\cdot 10 = 15\pi$.

Going around the 6 m wall leaves $4$ m of rope: a quarter circle of radius 4, length $2\pi$. Going around the 4 m wall leaves 6 m: a quarter circle of radius 6, length $3\pi$. These two quarter circles meet exactly at the far corner of the house ($4 + 6 = 10$).

The outer boundary of the region has length $15\pi + 2\pi + 3\pi = 20\pi$ m.

**Answer: (A) $20\pi$**

prompt: A trapezoid is formed by removing a corner from an equilateral triangle. Two copies of this trapezoid are placed side by side to form a parallelogram. The perimeter of the parallelogram exceeds the perimeter of the original triangle by 10 cm. What is the perimeter of the original equilateral triangle?

solutions.title: Name the sides
solutions.body:
Let the triangle have side $a$ and the removed equilateral corner side $b$. The trapezoid has sides $a$ (long base), $b$ (short base) and two legs $a - b$.

Placing two copies side by side (one turned upside down, joined along a leg) gives a parallelogram with sides $a + b$ and $a - b$. Its perimeter is $2(a + b) + 2(a - b) = 4a$.

$4a - 3a = a = 10$ cm, so the triangle's perimeter is $30$ cm (whatever $b$ is).

**Answer: (B) 30 cm**

prompt: A sequence of letters KANGAROOKANGAROO…KANGAROO contains 20 words KANGAROO. First, all letters in the odd positions of the sequence were erased. Then, in the sequence obtained, once again all the letters in the odd places were erased, and so on. At the very end, only one letter remained. What is this letter?

solutions.title: Powers of 2 survive
solutions.body:
After the first erasing only positions divisible by 2 remain, after the second only positions divisible by 4, and so on. The last letter left is at the position that is the largest power of 2 not exceeding $20\cdot 8 = 160$, namely $128$.

$128 = 16\cdot 8$ is the 8th letter of the 16th KANGAROO: **O**.

**Answer: (E) O**

prompt: What percent of the natural numbers from 1 to 10000 are perfect squares? (A perfect square is a number that can be written as the square of a natural number, for instance $100 = 10^2$.)
The number $8^8$ is obtained from the number $4^4$ by raising it to the power $n$. What is the number $n$?

A map of a neighbourhood is shown in the figure. The neighbourhood has the form of a right-angled triangle. All streets are shown on the map. They divide the neighbourhood into blocks that are also right-angled triangles. Alex wants to drive from the top endpoint of the neighbourhood to the rightmost endpoint. The traffic regulations only allow going down (vertically), right (horizontally), or down along the “hypotenuse” of a block (as in the small picture). How many different routes can Alex choose?

solutions.title: Count routes to every crossing
solutions.body:
Write at each crossing the number of ways to reach it: it is the sum of the numbers at the crossing above it, to its left, and diagonally up-left (where such streets exist). Row by row from the top (the triangle has legs of 4 blocks):
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}1\\1&2\\1&4&6\\1&6&16&22\\1&8&30&68&90\end{array}$$
For example $16 = 4 + 6 + 6$ and $68 = 16 + 22 + 30$. The rightmost corner gets $\mathbf{90}$.

**Answer: (D) 90**

prompt: The first digit of a 4-digit number is equal to the number of zeroes in this number. The second digit of the number is equal to the number of digits 1, the third digit is equal to the number of digits 2, and the fourth digit is the number of digits 3 in this number. How many numbers have this property?

A coin with a diameter of 1 cm rolls around the outside of a regular hexagon with a side length of 1 cm, as shown. What is the length (in cm) of the path traced out by the centre of the coin after one complete rotation around the hexagon?

solutions.title: Straight parts and arcs
solutions.body:
The centre stays at distance $r$ (the coin's radius) from the hexagon. Along each side it moves parallel to the side: $6\cdot 1 = 6$ cm. At each corner it turns around the vertex on an arc of radius $r$; the six turning angles add up to $360^\circ$, so the arcs together form one full circle of radius $r$, length $2\pi r$.

With diameter 1 cm, $r = \frac12$ cm, and the path has length $6 + 2\pi\cdot\frac12 = 6 + \pi$ cm.

**Answer: (B) $6+\pi$**

reviewNote: The official key gives D (6+2π), which would be the answer for a coin of radius 1 cm (probably the original wording). As printed (diameter 1 cm, matching the figure) the path is 6+π (B), which is used here.

prompt: Let $A$ be the least natural number with the following property: $10\times A$ is a perfect square and $6\times A$ is a perfect cube. How many positive divisors does the number $A$ have?

solutions.title: Exponents of 2, 3 and 5
solutions.body:
Only the primes 2, 3, 5 are needed: $A = 2^a3^b5^c$.
- $10A = 2^{a+1}3^b5^{c+1}$ is a square: $a+1$, $b$, $c+1$ even.
- $6A = 2^{a+1}3^{b+1}5^c$ is a cube: $a+1$, $b+1$, $c$ divisible by 3.

Smallest choices: $a + 1 = 6 \Rightarrow a = 5$; $b$ even with $b + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$: $b = 2$; $c$ odd and divisible by 3: $c = 3$.

$A = 2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5^3$ has $(5+1)(2+1)(3+1) = 72$ divisors.

**Answer: (D) 72**

prompt: At a party, five friends are going to give each other gifts in such a way that everybody gives one gift and receives one gift (of course, no one should receive their own gift). In how many ways is this possible?

solutions.title: Count by cycle structure
solutions.body:
Think of "who gives to whom" as arrows; everyone has one arrow out and one in, and nobody points to themselves. The arrows form cycles of length at least 2:
- one 5-cycle: $4! = 24$ ways;
- a 3-cycle and a 2-cycle: choose the pair, $\binom52 = 10$, and the 3-cycle can go 2 ways: $20$.

Total $24 + 20 = 44$.

**Answer: (C) 44**

solutions.title: Derangement recursion
solutions.body:
The number $D_n$ of such arrangements satisfies $D_n = (n-1)(D_{n-1} + D_{n-2})$ with $D_1 = 0$, $D_2 = 1$: $D_3 = 2$, $D_4 = 9$, $D_5 = 4(9 + 2) = 44$.

**Answer: (C) 44**

prompt: An equilateral triangle and a regular hexagon are inscribed in a circle, which itself is inscribed in a larger equilateral triangle (see the figure). $S_1$ denotes the area of the larger triangle, $S_2$ the area of the smaller triangle, and $S_3$ the area of the hexagon. Which of the following equalities is true?

solutions.title: Everything in terms of the radius
solutions.body:
Let the circle have radius $r$.
- The big triangle has inradius $r$, so its side is $2\sqrt3\,r$ and $S_1 = 3\sqrt3\,r^2$.
- The small triangle has circumradius $r$, so its side is $\sqrt3\,r$ and $S_2 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{4}r^2$.
- The hexagon consists of 6 equilateral triangles of side $r$: $S_3 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}r^2$.

Then $S_1 S_2 = \frac{27}{4}r^4 = S_3^2$, so $S_3 = \sqrt{S_1 S_2}$. (B gives $\frac{15\sqrt3}{8}r^2$, C gives $\frac{9\sqrt3}{4}r^2$, E gives $\frac{15\sqrt3}{4}r^2$ — all wrong.)

**Answer: (A) $S_3 = \sqrt{S_1\times S_2}$**

solutions.title: Ratios
solutions.body:
The small triangle has circumradius $r$, hence inradius $\frac r2$; the big one has inradius $r$. So the big triangle is the small one enlarged by factor 2: $S_1 = 4S_2$. The hexagon is the small triangle plus three caps, and each cap (a triangle with two hexagon sides) has the same area as one of the three triangles into which the centre cuts the small triangle; so $S_3 = 2S_2$. Hence $S_3^2 = 4S_2^2 = S_1S_2$.

**Answer: (A) $S_3 = \sqrt{S_1\times S_2}$**

prompt: It is 21:00 hours. I am driving at 100 km/h. At this speed I have enough gas to travel 80 km. The nearest gas station is 100 km away. The amount of gas my car uses per 1 km is proportional to the speed of the car. I want to reach the gas station as soon as possible. At what time, at the earliest, can I arrive at the gas station?

solutions.title: Fuel limits the speed
solutions.body:
Fuel per km is $kv$. The tank holds $80\cdot k\cdot 100 = 8000k$. Driving 100 km at constant speed $v$ uses $100kv$, so we need $100kv \le 8000k$, i.e. $v \le 80$ km/h.

(Varying the speed does not help: faster stretches cost more fuel per km than slower stretches save, so for a fixed amount of fuel the fastest way is a constant speed.) At 80 km/h the 100 km take $1.25$ h $= 1$ h 15 min: arrival at **22:15**.

**Answer: (B) 22:15**

prompt: There are three green, three red, three blue and three yellow cards in a box. The three cards of each colour are numbered 1, 2 and 3 (e.g. there is one green card with number 1, one green card with number 2, one green card with number 3, etc.). We take three cards from the box at random. Which of the following events is the most probable one?

choices.text: The three cards are of the same colour.
The three cards, regardless of their colours, have numbers 1, 2 and 3.
The three cards are of three different colours.
The three cards have the same number on them.
None of the above, the four previous events have the same probability.

solutions.title: Count the favourable triples
solutions.body:
There are $\binom{12}{3} = 220$ equally likely triples.
- A, same colour: 4 colours, 1 triple each: $4$.
- B, numbers 1, 2, 3: choose the colour of each number: $4^3 = 64$.
- C, three different colours: choose 3 colours ($4$ ways) and one of 3 cards in each: $4\cdot 27 = 108$.
- D, same number: 3 numbers, $\binom43 = 4$ ways each: $12$.

C is the most probable.

**Answer: (C) The three cards are of three different colours.**

prompt: A mathematically skilled spider spins a web and some of the strings have lengths as shown in the picture. If $x$ is an integer, determine the value of $x$.

solutions.title: Triangle inequality twice
solutions.body:
The string of length $x$ next to the centre of the web is a side of two small triangles:
- one with the other sides 9 and 5: $x < 9 + 5 = 14$;
- one with the other sides 5 and 17: $x > 17 - 5 = 12$.

So $12 < x < 14$ and the integer $x$ is $13$.

**Answer: (B) 13**

prompt: There are several necklaces in a safe deposit. All the necklaces have the same number of diamonds (at least two diamonds in each necklace). If the number of diamonds in the safe deposit were known, then the number of necklaces would also be certainly known. There are more than 200 and less than 300 diamonds in the safe. How many necklaces are there?

solutions.title: Only one factorisation
solutions.body:
If there are $N$ diamonds in $k \ge 2$ necklaces of $m \ge 2$ diamonds, then $N = km$. Knowing $N$ fixes $k$ only if $N$ has exactly one factorisation into two factors $\ge 2$ (as an ordered pair!). If $N = km$ with $k \ne m$ we could swap them; so the only factorisation must be $k = m = p$ with $p$ prime, i.e. $N = p^2$ (for $N = p^3$ we would also have $p\cdot p^2$).

The only square of a prime between 200 and 300 is $289 = 17^2$, so there are 17 necklaces.

**Answer: (B) 17**

prompt: Two circles have their centres on one of the diagonals of a square. They touch each other and the sides of the square, as shown. The square has a side length of 1 cm. What is the sum of the lengths of the two radii of the circles, in centimetres?

choices.text: It depends on the ratio of the two radii

solutions.title: Measure along the diagonal
solutions.body:
Let the radii be $r$ and $R$. The small circle touches the two sides at one corner, so its centre is $(r, r)$ — at distance $r\sqrt2$ from that corner along the diagonal. Likewise the other centre is $R\sqrt2$ from the opposite corner. The centres are $r + R$ apart (the circles touch). Along the diagonal of length $\sqrt2$:
$$r\sqrt2 + (r + R) + R\sqrt2 = \sqrt2 \;\Rightarrow\; (r+R)(1+\sqrt2) = \sqrt2,$$
$$r + R = \frac{\sqrt2}{1+\sqrt2} = \sqrt2(\sqrt2 - 1) = 2 - \sqrt2.$$
It does not depend on the ratio of the radii.

**Answer: (D) $2-\sqrt2$**
